1	# Frequency, phase and delay transfer {#sec-transfer-plan}
     2	
     3	A frequency plan can put every carrier in the intended band and still reverse a
     4	bearing, conjugate a modulation or change phase at each restart. The engineering
     5	question here is more specific: **what complex waveform does a declared RF input
     6	produce at the comparison record, in each identified state?** A useful answer is
     7	an annotated transfer law, with unwanted paths and validity conditions alongside
     8	it. A list of center frequencies is insufficient.
     9	
    10	We use the peak-voltage envelope and relative-phase ordering introduced in
    11	[Chapter 1](phase-comparison.qmd):
    12	$v_R(t)=\operatorname{Re}\{a(t)e^{j2\pi f_Rt}\}$ and channel $i$ relative to
    13	reference channel 0 means $\arg(z_i z_0^*)$. The Fourier kernel is
    14	$e^{-j2\pi ft}$. These remain local declared conventions, not new book-wide
    15	notation. The reader needs complex multiplication, physical delay and the
    16	finite-observation reasoning of [Chapter 3](observation-weighted-coherence.qmd).
    17	The sampling interface is ideal until explicitly qualified below; converter
    18	circuit design is not a prerequisite.
    19	
    20	By the end, an engineer should be able to trace a tone and a modulation sideband,
    21	calculate the output phase including reference paths, distinguish a constant
    22	phase correction from delay correction, locate image/alias exclusions, and name
    23	the state information required to compare records after reset. The worked plan
    24	will supply the transfer interface used by the conditional architecture in
    25	[Chapter 12](feasibility-architecture-allocations.qmd), without selecting hardware.
    26	
    27	## Conversion and reference signs {#sec-conversion-signs}
    28	
    29	Let the LO at mixer plane L be $2\cos(2\pi f_Lt+\lambda)$. The factor 2 simply
    30	normalizes this ideal mathematical multiplier to unit difference-band voltage
    31	gain; actual conversion gain has units, loading and drive conditions. Expand the
    32	real RF signal as one half of an analytic component plus its conjugate. The
    33	product contains components at $\pm(f_R+f_L)$ and $\pm(f_R-f_L)$.
    34	Selecting the **positive-frequency difference band**, with nonoverlapping bands,
    35	gives the following envelopes:
    36	
    37	$$
    38	b(t)=\begin{cases}
    39	 a(t)e^{-j\lambda},& f_R>f_L,\\
    40	 a^*(t)e^{j\lambda},& f_L>f_R.
    41	\end{cases}
    42	$$ {#eq-mixer-orientation}
    43	
    44	Thus high-side conversion conjugates an arbitrary complex modulation. This is
    45	not merely a minus sign attached to one test tone. For $a(t)=A e^{j2\pi\nu t}$,
    46	the high-side IF is centered at $f_L-f_R$ with offset $-\nu$ and envelope phase
    47	$-\arg A+\lambda$. For a phase-modulated waveform, every instantaneous modulation
    48	phase changes sign. For amplitude modulation with a real envelope, that inversion
    49	can be hidden by the test waveform.
    50	
    51	[Analog Devices MT-080, Rev. 0, pp. 1–3](https://www.analog.com/media/en/training-seminars/tutorials/MT-080.pdf)
    52	introduces sum/difference products and distinguishes high/low-side injection.
    53	Its ideal multiplier is not a guarantee of practical mixer gain or linearity.
    54	@eq-mixer-orientation is derived here with explicit envelope scaling.
    55	
    56	Our synthetic plan has $f_R=1.000$ GHz, $f_L=1.020$ GHz and positive IF center
    57	$f_I=20$ MHz. After a real IF filter with response $H(f)$, ideal real sampling at
    58	$F_s=100$ MHz and digital mixing by
    59	$e^{-j(\omega_0n+\chi)}$, $\omega_0=2\pi f_I/F_s$, the selected complex band
    60	has the high-side orientation. Conjugating that band once restores the RF
    61	orientation. For a single RF tone offset $\nu$, a physical RF delay $\tau_R$
    62	and constant LO/NCO phases, its main-path complex amplitude at output is
    63	
    64	$$
    65	Z(\nu)=A e^{-j2\pi(f_R+\nu)\tau_R}
    66	 H^*(f_I-\nu)e^{-j\lambda+j\chi}.
    67	$$ {#eq-restored-transfer}
    68	
    69	Here $A$ is the RF-plane peak phasor; any real positive scalar conversion gain
    70	has been factored out. The IF filter precedes sampling. In the worked digital FIR
    71	below, $H$ is instead its discrete-time steady response evaluated at analog
    72	frequency modulo $F_s$; this substitution is valid only for the declared ideal
    73	sampled path. Finite real-image terms are retained separately, rather than
    74	silently included in a scalar $H$.
    75	
    76	![Follow the waveform as well as its center frequency. The main-band drawing omits real mirror leakage; the finite-record equation below restores it. Scalar gain is factored out.](figures/frequency-transfer-orientation.svg){#fig-frequency-transfer-orientation fig-alt="Envelope path showing high-side conjugation, real sampling, FIR response, digital mixing and the final conjugation that restores RF orientation. LO and NCO phases enter at different planes."}
    77	
    78	The reference sensitivity follows directly. A positive LO phase perturbation
    79	appears as a **negative** restored output phase perturbation. If the LO source
    80	phase is $\lambda_s$ and its distribution delay is $\tau_L$, then
    81	$\lambda=\lambda_s-2\pi f_L\tau_L$. With NCO state held fixed,
    82	
    83	$$
    84	\delta\phi_i=-2\pi f_R\delta\tau_{R,i}
    85	 +2\pi f_L\delta\tau_{L,i}-\delta\lambda_s+\delta\chi_i
    86	$$ {#eq-transfer-path-sensitivity}
    87	
    88	at the center RF tone. Common $\lambda_s$ cancels in an ideal simultaneous
    89	relative comparison; unequal endpoint delays and their changes do not. Frequency
    90	conversion does not convert every physical delay into an IF-frequency phase
    91	error. The RF path is weighted by RF frequency and the LO path by LO frequency.
    92	
    93	Reference multiplication and division also carry phase. For an ideal harmonic
    94	multiplier of integer order $M$, a chosen harmonic has phase
    95	$M\phi+\phi_{M,0}$, including its additive phase error. An ideal divide-by-$N$
    96	output satisfies $N\theta=\phi$ modulo $2\pi$, so
    97	
    98	$$
    99	\theta=\frac{\phi}{N}+\frac{2\pi q}{N},\qquad q\in\{0,\ldots,N-1\}.
   100	$$
   101	
   102	The integer $q$ is an edge/state choice, not small noise. For centered small phase
   103	fluctuations within one known state, multiplication/division scales phase PSD by
   104	$M^2$ or $N^{-2}$ before additive disturbances; the offset-frequency variable is
   105	unchanged in this ideal phase-process model. This statement supplies neither a
   106	PLL transfer function nor deterministic divider initialization. A frequency
   107	relation alone leaves $q$ undetermined.
   108	
   109	## Bands and unwanted responses {#sec-frequency-exclusions}
   110	
   111	Before making a scalar transfer claim, list every physical path that reaches the
   112	observed band. For real sampling,
   113	$e^{j2\pi(f+kF_s)n/F_s}=e^{j2\pi fn/F_s}$ for integer $k$.
   114	The principal signed alias is $f_a=f-F_s\lfloor f/F_s+1/2\rfloor$ in
   115	$[-F_s/2,F_s/2)$. A real waveform also contains the negative-frequency conjugate.
   116	Folding to a positive plotted frequency therefore needs an additional orientation
   117	check. This algebra, rather than a mnemonic about Nyquist zones, determines the
   118	sign for an asymmetric modulation.
   119	
   120	[MT-002, Rev. A, pp. 9–11](https://www.analog.com/media/en/training-seminars/tutorials/MT-002.pdf)
   121	discusses zone inversion and analog filtering. Here alias placement is derived
   122	for an ideal sampler; aperture response, converter noise and distortion remain
   123	separate implementation inputs.
   124	
   125	For the plan above, consider a receiver passband of $\pm100$ kHz around the wanted
   126	carrier; the architecture's worked signal itself is a tone. The same digital band
   127	receives an RF image at $1.040$ GHz through the 20 MHz IF. A signal near 1.100 GHz
   128	produces an 80 MHz IF whose real sampled image lies at 20 MHz. The IF response
   129	must be evaluated at **80 MHz before sampling**, not 20 MHz after folding. Once
   130	these analog paths overlap in the samples, a downstream linear filter cannot
   131	separate arbitrary independent waveforms with identical sampled support.
   132	
   133	![The image sideband reverses relative to the wanted sideband. The illustrated 80 MHz alias suffers a second reversal and reaches the same restored offset as the wanted path. Band location is an exclusion requirement, not an attenuation measurement.](figures/frequency-exclusions.svg){#fig-frequency-exclusions fig-alt="Four frequency paths trace an RF sideband through positive IF, real-sampled folding and output orientation. Desired, image and alias paths overlap at the selected band; the blocker remains off-band."}
   134	
   135	A first spur inventory should likewise propagate candidate products
   136	$|m f_R\pm n f_L|$ through the sampler and digital selection. For example,
   137	$2f_L-2f_R=40$ MHz lies outside a 20 MHz IF passband, but other residual products overlap after sampling:
   138	
   139	| Residual analog product at the sampler | Frequency | Principal sampled alias | Consequence |
   140	|---|---:|---:|---|
   141	| RF + LO sum product | 2020 MHz | +20 MHz | Overlaps wanted; IF sum rejection required |
   142	| LO feedthrough | 1020 MHz | +20 MHz | Overlaps wanted; isolation/IF rejection required |
   143	| $2f_R-f_L$ nonlinear product | 980 MHz | −20 MHz | Real conjugate also overlaps; amplitude needs nonlinear evidence |
   144	
   145	Frequencies here are at nominal centers; propagate each product's actual
   146	sideband offsets and conjugations before accepting a modulation plan.
   147	The finite inventory $|m|,|n|\le2$ is a useful first check, not an
   148	exhaustive nonlinear model. Product amplitudes require part-specific drive,
   149	loading, compression, isolation and multi-signal evidence; integer labels do not
   150	predict them. Sum-band rejection and RF/IF image suppression must occur before
   151	those paths alias or overload a stage. Digital rejection cannot repair clipping.
   152	
   153	### A finite observation that can be exercised
   154	
   155	The architecture requires composite blocker-to-record voltage transfer no larger
   156	than $\eta_B=10^{-5}$, normalized to the wanted main response. Merely selecting
   157	10 MHz for a blocker and 20 MHz for the wanted IF does not establish this.
   158	At a noninteger record offset, a rectangular record leaks both real images.
   159	
   160	As a reproducible **operator candidate**, use a real three-tap FIR before digital
   161	mixing:
   162	
   163	$$
   164	h=[1,-2\cos(0.2\pi),1],\quad
   165	H(f)=e^{-j\omega}[2\cos\omega-2\cos(0.2\pi)],\quad
   166	\omega=2\pi f/F_s.
   167	$$ {#eq-three-tap-notch}
   168	
   169	It has a notch at 10 MHz and unit magnitude at 20 MHz. The latter response is
   170	$e^{j108^\circ}$, with group delay one sample in its nonzero, constant-sign band.
   171	The FIR needs two genuine preceding samples; discarding two initial outputs or
   172	supplying valid continuous history is part of the observation definition.
   173	
   174	Define the normalized record sum, for $N=100000$ samples, $T=N/F_s=1$ ms,
   175	
   176	$$
   177	D_N(f)=\frac1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}e^{j2\pi fn/F_s}
   178	 =e^{j\pi(N-1)f/F_s}\frac{\sin(\pi Nf/F_s)}{N\sin(\pi f/F_s)}.
   179	$$
   180	
   181	At integer multiples of $F_s$, use the continuous limit 1. A real tone with
   182	positive-frequency peak phasor $B$ after conversion but before this FIR gives,
   183	**before final conjugation**,
   184	
   185	$$
   186	Y=e^{-j\chi}\{B H(f)D_N(f-f_I)
   187	 +B^* H^*(f)D_N(-f-f_I)\}.
   188	$$ {#eq-real-record}
   189	
   190	This follows by substituting $x[n]=(B e^{j2\pi fn/F_s}+B^*e^{-j2\pi fn/F_s})/2$
   191	into $2N^{-1}\sum(h*x)[n]e^{-j(\omega_0n+\chi)}$.
   192	No random phase or favorable cancellation was assumed. Final $Z=Y^*$.
   193	The second term explains why the exact finite real observation is generally a
   194	map in both $B$ and $B^*$, rather than a complex scalar gain alone.
   195	
   196	For wanted and blocker RF offsets each in $[-100,100]$ Hz, put
   197	$f_w=20\text{ MHz}-\delta_w$ and $f_b=10\text{ MHz}-\delta_b$.
   198	At the worst offset, $|H(f_b)|\le7.387\times10^{-6}$. If the middle coefficient
   199	has error $|\epsilon_c|\le10^{-6}$, its additional response has magnitude at
   200	most $10^{-6}$. Meanwhile the two blocker sums obey
   201	
   202	$$
   203	|D_N(f_b-f_I)|+|D_N(-f_b-f_I)|<1.383\times10^{-5}.
   204	$$
   205	
   206	To check this bound without a sweep, each numerator is at most $\sin(0.1\pi)$;
   207	the two denominator sine magnitudes are at least
   208	$\sin[\pi(0.1-10^{-6})]$ and $\sin[\pi(0.3-10^{-6})]$, respectively.
   209	The wanted main coefficient is greater than 0.9836 including this coefficient
   210	error. Thus the **sum** of blocker-path magnitudes relative to that main path is
   211	less than $1.3\times10^{-10}$ in this steady, exact-arithmetic model, comfortably
   212	below the supplied $10^{-5}$ interface. The wanted mirror/main ratio is bounded
   213	by $3.4\times10^{-6}$; it is a separate signal-dependent error, not blocker
   214	rejection. Its per-channel phase magnitude is at most $\arcsin(3.4\times10^{-6})$,
   215	about $0.000195^\circ$, and it must be charged if retained.
   216	
   217	![The center null alone proves little. Offset bounds, coefficient error, both real images and the finite observation produce the stated rejection envelope. The plotted exact center is clipped at −130 dB for display; its mathematical value is zero.](figures/notch-observation.svg){#fig-notch-observation fig-alt="Notch magnitude versus a small blocker frequency offset, showing the exact coefficient and a coefficient-error envelope, followed by the finite-observation rejection conditions."}
   218	
   219	This example provides an executable transfer, not a selected filter or deployed
   220	rejection guarantee. It omits arithmetic roundoff/overflow, reset transients,
   221	additional analog aliases/spurs and clock error. The FIR changes noise transfer;
   222	the architecture's effective $N_0$ must refer to this complete observation or be
   223	recomputed from source spectra. It cannot simply be copied from a different
   224	filter. Two delays and one constant multiply per input sample imply roughly
   225	300 million constant multiplies/s for three 100 MS/s channels before any
   226	optimization, plus the digital mixer/accumulation. Symmetry and fixed coefficients
   227	may reduce cost; no implementation/power claim follows. The two-sample history
   228	adds 20 ns of startup data, distinct from the FIR's 10 ns group delay and from
   229	processing/transport latency. Those distinctions matter to the 0.6 ms processing
   230	and 2.5 W envelopes in Chapter 12.
   231	
   232	## Response over bandwidth {#sec-transfer-bandwidth}
   233	
   234	Take the worked input tone phase $25^\circ$, RF delay $\tau_R=25$ ps,
   235	LO phase $\lambda=17^\circ$ at L and NCO phase $\chi=11^\circ$ at the defined
   236	sample origin. @eq-restored-transfer gives at the carrier
   237	
   238	$$
   239	\phi_Z=25^\circ-9^\circ-17^\circ-108^\circ+11^\circ=-98^\circ.
   240	$$
   241	
   242	For an RF sideband at $\nu=+50$ kHz, the IF is 19.95 MHz. Its FIR phase is
   243	$108.18^\circ$, while the RF delay contributes $-9.00045^\circ$.
   244	The restored tone therefore has offset **+50 kHz** and phase
   245	$-98.18045^\circ$ at the declared origin. An independent real-waveform
   246	mix/filter/sample calculation tests this result; an amplitude-only test cannot
   247	show its orientation.
   248	
   249	For a smooth nonzero main transfer $G(\nu)$, define equivalent envelope group
   250	delay as $\tau_g=-[2\pi]^{-1}d\arg G/d\nu$. Because
   251	$G(\nu)=e^{-j2\pi(f_R+\nu)\tau_R}H^*(f_I-\nu)$ up to constant reference phases,
   252	the two reversals give
   253	
   254	$$
   255	\tau_g(\nu)=\tau_R+\tau_{g,H}(f_I-\nu).
   256	$$
   257	
   258	For this FIR, it is $10.025$ ns. The carrier phase intercept is **not**
   259	$-2\pi f_R\tau_g$: the RF carrier and IF filter use different frequency origins.
   260	A single-tone calibration removes an intercept but cannot establish the slope.
   261	A differential slope $\Delta\tau$ produces phase error
   262	$-2\pi\nu\Delta\tau$ after center correction; a $0.1^\circ$ limit at
   263	$|\nu|=100$ kHz requires $|\Delta\tau|\le2.778$ ns under a pure-delay model.
   264	
   265	Nor does unit magnitude imply undistorted modulation. Consider a further
   266	orientation-restored equivalent all-pass response
   267	$Q(\nu)=(1-j\nu/f_p)/(1+j\nu/f_p)$, $f_p=100$ kHz. It has magnitude 1,
   268	phase $-2\arctan(\nu/f_p)$ and delay
   269	$1/[\pi f_p(1+(\nu/f_p)^2)]$. At 50 kHz its phase is $-53.130^\circ$,
   270	whereas extrapolating its center delay predicts $-57.296^\circ$.
   271	The $4.166^\circ$ discrepancy affects relative sideband timing and waveform shape.
   272	This is a stable causal first-order all-pass in the equivalent complex path,
   273	not a specified RF component. A sweep or known asymmetric modulation is needed
   274	to assess dispersion; a flat level response and a center phase correction miss it.
   275	
   276	![Phase intercept, phase slope and curvature answer different engineering questions. Synthetic exact transfer curves illustrate why equal carrier phase and equal magnitude do not ensure equal modulation transfer.](figures/transfer-response.svg){#fig-transfer-response fig-alt="Two plots compare orientation-restored phase and group delay of the basic RF/FIR path with the same path plus a unity-magnitude all-pass. The all-pass curves expose dispersion hidden by a center-tone calibration."}
   277	
   278	## State-sensitive plans {#sec-transfer-states}
   279	
   280	A plan has state coordinates as well as frequencies. In this example record the
   281	LO/divider state, actual sample origin, NCO accumulator phase, filter history and
   282	calibration reference planes. A positive one-sample shift means that sample
   283	label $n$ now contains the old waveform at $n+1$ while the NCO label remains $n$.
   284	Before restoration that advances a 20 MHz IF by $72^\circ$; after conjugation it
   285	changes output phase by **−72°**. If the NCO/sample labels shift consistently,
   286	the result differs: specify what moved before correcting it. A +90° NCO phase
   287	change gives +90° restored phase. A divide-by-2 reference state change can give
   288	180° LO change, hence −180° output change. Equal output frequencies in all three
   289	cases do not imply a valid comparison to the prior calibration.
   290	
   291	Actual hardware documentation makes these conditions concrete.
   292	[AD9208 Rev. 0, p. 49 and pp. 78–81](https://www.analog.com/media/en/technical-documentation/data-sheets/AD9208.pdf)
   293	separately describes NCO-accumulator synchronization, link latency, SYSREF timing
   294	and multichip alignment. Its p. 49 SPI reset method is limited to NCOs on one
   295	chip; the SYSREF method has enabling conditions. Page 78 requires distribution
   296	skew, setup/hold and link-latency conditions. This is evidence of conditional
   297	state mechanisms in that device/revision, not evidence that our synthetic
   298	100 MS/s plan uses it or has deterministic RF phase. The p. 80 timestamp-mode
   299	paragraph also contains apparently conflicting reset wording; no reset guarantee
   300	is imported from it. Consult the relevant revision and implementation evidence
   301	before depending on a mode.
   302	
   303	Calibration should exercise what the measurement needs. A known RF phase change
   304	at plane R tests conversion orientation; a positive frequency-offset change tests
   305	modulation orientation and slope. A coherent RF sweep can identify differential
   306	transfer over the usable band. Injection after an RF selector cannot identify
   307	its phase, and no electronic injection establishes the antenna's field response.
   308	A restart test must retain sample identity and reference/NCO state evidence, and
   309	must distinguish constant offsets from invalid or settling records. These are
   310	verification implications of the transfer, not a complete transition procedure.
   311

# Founding Charter — Coherent Receiver Theory and Design

**Status:** governing project intent; technical implementation choices below are provisional until specifically accepted.

## Mission
Develop an exceptionally comprehensive, mathematically rigorous, scientifically defensible and practically applicable advanced engineering **textbook and reference** on coherent receiver theory and engineering. The audience is experienced RF engineers, including engineers with little previous specialization in coherent receivers. Codex CLI is the principal AI-assisted development environment, **not** the book's primary audience.

## Primary success criterion
After systematic end-to-end study, a qualified RF engineer should be able to approach unfamiliar coherent receiver development problems and proceed from operational need through requirements, feasibility, architecture selection, system budgets, subsystem design, synchronization, calibration, physical implementation, integration, verification and production planning, using this book as the **primary technical and methodological reference**. Component-specific information, current standards and specialized implementation details may require external sources. The book must not omit essential coherent-receiver-specific reasoning and expect the reader to reconstruct it elsewhere.

## The kind of book
- Advanced, coherent textbook **and** practical engineering design handbook.
- First principles where consequential, with derivations, assumptions, limiting cases, physical interpretation and applicability conditions.
- Integrated system reasoning: why subsystem interactions and correlations determine achievable performance.
- Learning sequence for a human engineer and practical reference navigation for future use.
- Genuine generalization to unfamiliar requirements and architectures, not memorization of worked examples.
- Contrast idealized models with nonideal hardware, calibration limitations, actual waveforms, instrument limitations and production variability.

## Required domain breadth
1. Operational needs, systems methods, specifications, feasibility and traceability.
2. Coherence definitions; complex signals, stochastic phase, correlation, spectra, estimation and synchronization.
3. Receiver architecture, frequency planning, noise, linearity, dynamic range and system error budgets.
4. RF and analog frontend, frequency conversion, synthesizers, LO/clock/reference distribution.
5. Data conversion, I/Q, digital downconversion, timing and carrier recovery, FPGA/processor consequences.
6. Multichannel coherence, amplitude/phase/delay alignment, observability, calibration and drift.
7. PCB, power, signal integrity, EMI, thermal, mechanical and environmental implementation.
8. Analytical/computational modeling, sensitivities, uncertainty, verification and measurement.
9. Manufacturing, production test, yield, reliability, configuration and lifecycle.
10. Carrier-coherent communications, arrays/DF, coherent radar/sensing and phase measurement applications.

This list describes coverage goals, **not** the final table of contents.

## Rigorous technical standards
Distinguish mathematical correctness, computational implementation correctness, physical validity, engineering adequacy and demonstrated compliance. Never claim a model is physically validated because its software tests pass. Distinguish one-/two-sided spectra, reference planes, phase accuracy/stability/repeatability, common/differential errors, deterministic/stochastic behavior, observation time, operating state and calibration dependence. Define uncertainty and identify incomplete evidence. Source citations must support the actual claims and not be fabricated.

## Scope control without dilution
- Full internal development for essential coherent-receiver reasoning.
- Selective internal development for adjacent supporting disciplines.
- Established general engineering theory and device-specific facts may be referenced externally.
- Evaluate adequacy by conceptual understanding **and** the ability to calculate, make design decisions and verify them.
- Use complete reference designs plus contrasting cases and failure analyses to check generalizability.
- Do not use page count or number of generated files as a quality metric.

## Human authority and completion
Codex may draft, research, derive, compute, check and identify issues. It cannot approve consequential engineering results on its own. Acceptance needs suitable evidence and human technical review for the declared use. Acceptance is scoped and revisable, not infallibility. Material may be released in usable intermediate editions with explicit limitations.

## Development philosophy
Use bounded technical units, minimum sufficient assurance, continuous readable outputs, consistent notation, source provenance and modest version-controlled evidence. Avoid large knowledge graphs, custom publishing engines and autonomous multi-agent infrastructure until warranted. Technical quality is uncompromising; process complexity should be proportionate.

## Immediate sequence
1. Develop the foundational reader competence and engineering capability inventory.
2. Use it with candidate reference designs to establish technical scope, dependencies and a provisional intellectual architecture.
3. Evaluate mathematical authoring/publishing tools through a genuine pilot.
4. Develop a pilot on relative phase stability in a two-channel coherent receiver from observable requirement through model, architecture choices and verification plan.
5. Revise the development system on evidence, then author progressively.

## Original intent and authority
This charter consolidates the user's clarified objective and agreed development philosophy. It does **not** claim that an inventory, chapter, design, calculation, physical model or review has been technically accepted. Requirements of the book are distinguished from provisional toolchain and repository choices in `project/decisions/`.
# Technical Coverage, Canonical Treatments and Capability Support

**Status:** development specification produced on 2026-10-28; provisionally accepted by the project owner on 2026-10-29 for book architecture, annotated table-of-contents and intellectual-organization planning under [ADR-0003](decisions/ADR-0003-provisional-architecture-acceptance.md), subject to its four review qualifications. The [inventory](competence-inventory.md) owns capability definitions and their required competence dimensions. The [design briefs and stress tests](reference-design-plan.md) challenge this specification. No technical treatment specified here has thereby been derived, implemented, physically validated or accepted.

## 1. Reading the coverage specification

K01–K26 identify shared treatments; A35–A41 identify application-specific mappings. These are Markdown navigation labels, not book numbering or a knowledge database. A treatment is bounded by a reasoning responsibility, not by page count. Suffixes a/b/c distinguish first treatment from refinement only where prerequisites differ. Dependencies are owned by §3, not inferred from identifier order.

Every treatment below requires a human-readable explanation, applicable mathematics, physical interpretation, a consequential calculation/decision, limitations and an assessment. Statements such as “derive,” “evaluate,” and “implement” specify future book obligations; they do not report work performed at this architecture stage.

**F/S/E** mean full internal / selective supporting / external treatment. F applies to essential coherent reasoning even where an adjacent discipline is S or E. Every imported fact must retain units, definitions, conditions and evidence limits. Shared source-path calculations must identify the observable, reference planes, waveform, observation filtering, time interval, operating state and calibration dependency wherever consequential.

**Evidence boundary:** this package analyzes the repository's planning requirements. It introduces no newly verified technical source claims. The existing [source examination note](../references/source-notes/competence-inventory-foundations.md) supports only its recorded S1–S9 distinctions; those passages were not re-examined here. Its evidence cannot certify the treatments below. §6 identifies required later research and review. No universal formula, PSD normalization, product requirement or current device guarantee is selected.

## 2. Canonical development obligations

### K01 — Operational observables and coherent representations

**Canonical result:** consistent conversion between physical waveforms, phasors, analytic signals, complex envelopes and sampled representations, with explicit power/phase/frequency conventions. Develop phase, frequency, delay, correlation and observation definitions; separate accuracy, temporal stability, restart repeatability and alignment. **Use/assessment:** reconstruct a waveform, follow conjugation/inversion and compare two differently filtered or referenced measurands. **Limits:** phase near amplitude nulls, wrapped versus unwrapped quantities, undefined absolute references and unresolved normalization. **Depth:** F coherent representations and reference changes; S Fourier refresher; E missing general RF remediation. K03 owns stochastic observation analysis; K22 owns instrument realization.

### K02 — Scalar stochastic and complex phase reasoning

**Canonical result:** probability/expectation and scalar covariance bridges; random processes, stationarity/ergodicity, complex proper/improper models, circular statistics and phase increments. Develop multiplicative complex phase versus additive noise, including the local additive-noise-to-phase relation and its breakdown. **Use/assessment:** compare disturbances with equal marginal phase variance and different temporal structure, construct a justified scalar model and identify unsupported Gaussian/independence assumptions. **Limits:** low SNR, fades, nonstationarity, higher moments and phase wrapping. **Depth:** F coherent stochastic reasoning; S general probability. Physical source construction belongs to K09, not a postulated correlation coefficient.

### K03 — Spectra, finite observation and coherence

**Canonical result:** auto/cross spectra, observation/window/filter weighting, phase/frequency/time relations, phase-increment and complex-coherence relationships, finite-record bias/variance and stability measures. Develop shared-source differential transfer through unequal paths, including the pure-delay limit. Identify exactly where Gaussian, stationary, small-angle or fourth-moment assumptions enter. **Use/assessment:** compare spectral/time formulations and equal-marginal-variance cases; evaluate averaging uncertainty and convergence. **Limits:** unqualified PSD integrals, nonstationary/distributional spectra, finite bandwidth and effective independent samples. **Depth:** F essential relations; S broader estimator catalogue. Matrix forms add K04; A39 owns application correlation sensitivity.

### K04 — Matrix inference and coupled response

**Canonical result:** complex vectors/matrices, covariance and quadratic forms, rank, eigenstructure, singular values, least squares, conditioning and justified constraints/regularization. **Use/assessment:** form a channel model, identify null directions and quantify sensitivity; check covariance symmetry and positive semidefiniteness. **Limits:** formal inversion versus stable inference, coordinate/reference freedoms and poorly determined physical inputs. **Depth:** S linear-algebra bridge; F coherent uses. K09 supplies physically constructed covariance; K05 owns inferential interpretation and K20 owns correction realizability.

### K05 — Parameter inference, information and ambiguity

**Canonical result:** representative phase/frequency/delay/amplitude estimation from likelihood and least squares, nuisance parameters, bias/variance, applicable information bounds and global ambiguity. Start with scalar inference; extend to coupled parameters with K04. **Use/assessment:** derive/evaluate an estimator and bound, exhibit indistinguishable parameter sets, then test mismatch and local versus global conclusions. **Limits:** regularity conditions, finite observations, low-SNR/threshold behavior, ambiguity and model error. **Depth:** F receiver-specific inference; S statistical theory. Calibration measurement freedoms belong to K21a; system feasibility to K11.

### K06 — Acquisition, tracking and desired-signal transfer

**Canonical result:** detector/loop dynamics, locked-state transfer, stability/noise bandwidth, sampled latency and dynamic stress; separate nonlinear acquisition, slips, saturation and recovery. Derive transfer of the wanted physical signal as well as nuisance disturbances. **Use/assessment:** evaluate and realize a bounded acquisition/tracking procedure including holdover and reacquisition; compare feedforward/feedback alternatives. **Limits:** no capture guarantee from linear locked-state analysis; faded or ambiguous observations and delayed feedback. **Depth:** F coherent synchronization; S control bridge. K23 owns system transition sequencing; K21c owns maintenance policy.

### K07 — Approximation, uncertainty and adequate models

**Canonical result:** dimensional and limiting-case reasoning, perturbation/sensitivity, covariance-aware uncertainty propagation, numerical convergence/precision, and nonlinear/ambiguous alternatives to first-order propagation. Develop model hierarchy and discrepancy separately from numerical error. **Use/assessment:** construct and execute a bounded analytical/computational model for a decision, compare independent formulations and state unsupported extrapolations. **Limits:** uncertain parameters, wrong physics, nonlinearity and circular validation. **Depth:** F coherent interpretation/model assessment; S general numerical tools; E tool particulars. K13 owns allocations, K22 measurement uncertainty and K25 evidence decisions; they reuse this mathematics.

### K08 — Propagation, geometry and physical transduction

**Canonical result:** phase/delay/Doppler and minimum vector field-to-port/sensor models, with bases, reference geometry, effective response, loading/coupling and cross-polar leakage. Derive the conditions for a scalar channel model. **Use/assessment:** calculate direction/frequency/polarization or sensor dependence and show which external-path changes internal injection cannot establish. **Limits:** narrowband/far-field/quasi-static assumptions, multipath, geometry and nuisance transduction. **Depth:** F minimum receiver model; S supporting fields/propagation; E full-wave radiators, detailed environments and specialist sensor laws. Externally supplied models must expose uncertainty and conventions.

### K09 — Physical disturbance generation and paths

**Canonical result:** convert physical thermal/representative active-device and external-field noise through loaded/coupled networks into delivered spectra and covariance. Develop reciprocal mixing with effective LO spectra, blocker/preselection/observation filtering and internal branch contributions; develop timing-error disturbance from the complete analog waveform and clock process. **Use/assessment:** calculate narrow-blocker/flat-spectrum limits and finite-spectrum contrasts; construct coupled covariance and derive filter/LO/clock constraints. **Limits:** source independence, impedance/power normalization, stationarity, small timing errors and unavailable physical parameters. **Depth:** F coherent source/path reasoning; S noise-network bridge; E detailed device physics and verified parameters. K13 assembles, rather than regenerates, these contributions.

### K10 — Detection, integration and signal-preserving rejection

**Canonical result:** correlation/matched filtering, applicable sufficient-statistic/likelihood reasoning, colored-noise weighting, coherent/noncoherent accumulation and reference mismatch. Develop separation/degree-of-freedom limits and effects of contaminated training or reference leakage. **Use/assessment:** realize and evaluate a bounded extraction/rejection method, calculating retained desired information, detection/correlation outcome and uncertainty. **Limits:** indistinguishable subspaces, finite support, covariance conditioning and pre-digital clipping. **Depth:** F coherent extraction/rejection; S general detection theory; E exhaustive adaptive/mission algorithms. Applications own their hypotheses, waveform mappings and task consequences.

### K11 — Requirements, joint feasibility and architecture selection

**First treatment:** formulate operational needs, states, observables, missing limits and evidence routes. **Quantitative refinement:** intersect information, ambiguity, energy/bandwidth/time, dynamics, headroom, latency and technology/resource constraints; distinguish empty, conditional and evidenced feasible regions. **Use/assessment:** calculate gain-range and information/steering conflicts, compare architectures and quantitative interfaces, identify which change restores feasibility. **Limits:** local precision is not global acquisition; supplied technology envelopes are assumptions until evidenced. **Depth:** F coherent systems reasoning; S generic systems/constrained analysis; E actual contracts, regulations and device facts. K13/subsystem results refine the initial feasible region through engineering interaction.

### K12 — End-to-end frequency, phase and delay transfer

**Canonical result:** phase signs and reference transfer through conversion, multiplication/division, filtering and sampling; desired/image/alias/spur bands, spectral inversion and group delay. **Use/assessment:** construct and exercise an annotated frequency/reference plan across states, tracking tones/modulation and identifying reset-sensitive elements. **Limits:** ideal transfer versus stateful/nonlinear hardware, constant phase versus frequency-dependent response. **Depth:** F coherent transfer; S conventional frequency-plan refresher. K15 and K17/K19 provide implementation refinements; K23 manages transitions. Sampling placement can first use a declared ideal interface rather than converter design as a prerequisite.

### K13 — Correlated allocations and budget closure

**Canonical result:** propagate physical source/path results, covariance/cross-spectra and deterministic terms to task observables; distinguish margin, variability, model/parameter uncertainty, calibration residual and measurement uncertainty. **Use/assessment:** calculate closure and sensitivity to a correlation, blocker, environment or missing parameter; compare with K11 feasibility. **Limits:** double counting common sources, incorrect independence, wrong reference planes and missing application mappings. **Depth:** F coherent allocations; S generic budgeting. Application limits and subsystem transfer specifications may be supplied initially, with explicit later reconciliation.

### K14 — Analog information preservation, nonlinearity and gain policy

**Canonical result:** gain/filter/isolation/headroom design under the full signal/blocker envelope, adequate memoryless/dynamic/measured nonlinear models, AM-to-AM/PM, crest factor, gain-state complex response and recovery. **Use/assessment:** calculate stage allocations and realize a bounded gain/valid-data policy; compare weak-signal/blocker, modulated/multitone and strong-pulse cases. **Limits:** IP2/IP3 extrapolation, memory, overload and missing loading/drive/bias evidence. **Depth:** F coherent nonlinear reasoning; S circuit design; E part/revision/operating guarantees or characterization. Converter interfaces, state and calibration access are reconciled with K17/K23/K21 rather than assumed solved.

### K15 — Synthesis and endpoint reference distribution

**First treatment (a):** PLL/reference/oscillator transfer, multiplication/division, noise/spurs, tuning/settling and state-dependent synthesis. **Endpoint refinement (b):** source-sharing through unequal branch response, additive branch noise, loading/isolation, environmental sensitivity and actual endpoint comparison. **Use/assessment:** derive an effective LO envelope from blocker conditions, compare synthesis/topology alternatives and evaluate endpoint evidence including test-reference correlation. **Limits:** frequency accuracy does not establish phase; typical data and source-sharing are not guarantees. **Depth:** F coherent synthesis/distribution; S oscillator/interconnect theory; E technology-specific guarantees. K16 owns remote inference; K23 owns sequencing.

### K16 — Distributed clock and carrier-reference inference

**Canonical result:** offset/rate/drift and one-/two-way measurement equations with propagation/equipment delays, reference freedoms, reciprocity/asymmetry and modulo-cycle ambiguity. Distinguish RF phase, frequency, sample epoch and transport latency. **Use/assessment:** evaluate an ambiguity/asymmetry case and bounded alignment/holdover/recovery method; calculate residuals and valid outage intervals separately. **Limits:** missing geometry/delay information, delayed-feedback stability and uncertain link conditions. **Depth:** F minimum distributed inference; S representative transfer methods; E protocols/hardware. Digital resampling is a conditional realization using K19, not a prerequisite for continuous reference equations.

### K17 — Sampling, timing and converter feasibility

**Canonical result:** bandpass/aliasing and anti-alias interfaces, aperture jitter/skew with correlations, quantization-model conditions, nonlinear/interleaving effects and conditional dither. **Use/assessment:** calculate rate, headroom, clock and driver/converter requirements for broadband, coherent low-level, blocker and recovery cases, not only a tone. **Limits:** total-waveform timing sensitivity, correlated quantization, front-end distortion, loading/common-mode/settling and typical-versus-guaranteed evidence. **Depth:** F coherent converter consequences; S converter theory; E device data/errata. K09 owns timing-disturbance construction; K14 analog interface results interact with selection.

### K18 — Quadrature and conjugate-response fidelity

**Canonical result:** frequency/state-dependent I/Q imbalance, improper/conjugate signal models, DC offset, leakage and desired near-DC response. **Use/assessment:** estimate/apply a bounded correction and evaluate independent swept/modulated/near-DC data with level/state variation. **Limits:** suppression of a real signal, ambiguous leakage and unsupported correction envelope. **Depth:** F coherent I/Q reasoning; E device internals. Analog quadrature does not require ADC/DDC knowledge. Digital correction adds K17/K19; general calibration validity comes from K21b.

### K19 — Multirate processing and finite-resource realization

**First treatment (a):** DDC/NCO, filtering/channelization, decimation/resampling, phase/delay, sample identity, transients and asynchronous timing estimates. **Realization (b):** numerical scaling, fixed/floating precision, overflow, coefficient error, throughput, buffering, clock-domain crossing and timestamps. **Use/assessment:** realize a bounded chain with impulse/tone/modulated and rate/reset tests; compare reference calculations and establish platform timing/resources. **Limits:** finite length, noise enhancement, startup state, lost samples and unsupported hardware claims. **Depth:** F coherent processing/resource consequences; S DSP/digital design; E HDL/core/tool details. K20 owns general correction feasibility; K23 integrates state.

### K20 — Complex-response alignment and correction feasibility

**Canonical result:** relative amplitude/phase/delay/dispersion response and physically meaningful inverse approximation; distinguish identifiable parameters, feasible compensation and irretrievable information. Develop causality/stability/minimum-phase implications, finite latency/length, coefficient range/resolution and noise gain before choosing analog/digital realization. **Use/assessment:** calculate wideband alignment residuals and deep-attenuation/null contrasts; compare prevention, approximate correction and architecture change before irreversible combination. **Limits:** clipping/aliasing/rank loss without extra information; a notch is not automatically irrecoverable. **Depth:** F correction reasoning; S necessary systems/inverse bridge. K19 supplies digital realization only where selected; K21 owns estimation procedure and validity.

### K21 — Calibration observability, procedure and maintenance

**First treatment (a):** measurement equations, stimulus/reference uncertainty, nuisance/reference freedoms, rank, omitted paths and desired-observable preservation. **Procedure (b):** combine metrology with observable parameters and feasible correction; acquire, estimate, apply and evaluate held-out residuals, noise gain, coefficient resources and provenance across states/band/environment. **Maintenance (c):** derive cadence, latency, downtime, drift/motion/outage policy and wanted-versus-nuisance transfer; reject invalid compensation or declare degraded operation. **Use/assessment:** demonstrate an indistinguishable calibration case, an executable bounded correction and an independent validity/retained-signal test. **Depth:** F all coherent reasoning; E instrument commands/specialist environmental inputs. A small fit residual is insufficient.

### K22 — Operational metrology and uncertainty

**Canonical result:** instrument measurement equations including intentional method dependence, loading, fixtures, de-embedding, corrections, correlated references, floor/dynamic range, finite-record uncertainty and traceability. Reuse K07 propagation rather than create a second uncertainty theory. **Use/assessment:** execute or critically evaluate supplied measurements, calculate uncertainty and change reference/fixture topology to test sensitivity. **Limits:** apparent cancellation, instrument floors, estimator bias, insufficient degrees of freedom and nonlinear/ambiguous propagation. **Depth:** F coherent metrology; S general measurement methods; E instrument/calibration-standard particulars. K21a is conditional where calibration observability is needed; executable calibration is not prerequisite to the first measurement treatment.

### K23 — State causality, integration and diagnosis

**First treatment (a):** initialization/reset/retune/link/reference-loss causality across applicable PLL/divider/sampler/FIFO/NCO/filter states; separate sample epoch, transport latency and RF phase. **Integration (b):** interfaces, sequencing, channel/sample identity, calibration/configuration versions, logging and valid-data gates. **Diagnosis (c):** discriminate physical hypotheses by controlled substitutions and interventions, preserving raw data and state. **Use/assessment:** implement/exercise bounded transitions and fault cases and interpret exposure/confidence through K25; evaluate a discriminating diagnostic experiment. **Depth:** F coherent state/diagnosis; S software/configuration practice; E device-specific state guarantees. No universal digital chain is assumed.

### K24 — Physical and environmental realization

**First treatment (a):** translate sensitivity allocations into routing, return-current, power/filter, shielding, coupling/isolation and test-access constraints; calculate representative aggressor/supply-to-phase paths. **Environmental refinement (b):** thermal coefficients/gradients/time constants, strain, vibration, connectors, warmup and mitigation residuals. **Use/assessment:** evaluate concrete implementation constraints and controlled aggressor/gradient/handling evidence. **Limits:** equal physical lengths, uniform chamber results and generic layout rules do not establish electrical matching or field validity. **Depth:** F coherent consequences; S SI/PI/EMI/thermal/mechanical bridges; E materials/fabrication/qualification facts. Correction interface may be supplied before maintenance policy is developed.

### K25 — Verification coverage and bounded evidence decisions

**Canonical result:** requirement-to-evidence tracing, operating/state/environment coverage, uncertainty decision rules and justified finite exposure/statistical bounds for rare failures under stated dependence assumptions. **Use/assessment:** evaluate cases near a limit and identify untested corners, false conclusions and additional evidence needed. **Limits:** zero observed failures, model/software correctness, prototype success and physical applicability are distinct claims. **Depth:** F coherent verification; S assurance/sampling methods; E mandated compliance standards. K22 supplies measurement evidence; K07 assesses model adequacy. Application observables and actual configuration define the scope of any compliance claim.

### K26 — Production feasibility and continued validity

**Production (a):** joint unit/lot/process variation and environmental residuals, coefficient range/resolution, fixture uncertainty, calibration/test sweep/settling/retest time, coverage reduction and escapes/false rejects. **Service (b):** aging, monitoring, reference health, replacements/updates and calibration invalidation/requalification. **Use/assessment:** calculate bounded joint yield/test effort, vary unsupported distributions/correlations and evaluate a repaired/updated configuration. **Limits:** a prototype is not a distribution; unknown lifetime/variation cannot support numerical reliability/yield claims. **Depth:** F coherent lifecycle decisions; S statistical manufacturing/reliability; E supplier/process/lifetime facts. Preserve uncertainty and raw configuration evidence from K21–K25.

### Duplication and fragmentation controls

- K01 defines the observable; K03 develops stochastic observation; K22 realizes measurement; A41 designs the reporting instrument. Cross-reference those roles instead of redefining “phase stability” locally.
- K02/K04 define stochastic/matrix tools; K09 constructs physical sources; K13 allocates their consequences. A covariance spreadsheet is not a replacement for source physics.
- K05 owns general inference; K21a calibration freedoms; K20 feasible correction; K21b the executed procedure. Their assessments must demonstrate all four responsibilities separately.
- K06 owns loop and desired-signal transfer; K23 system state causality; K21c continuing validity. An implementation state machine cannot substitute for acquisition mathematics.
- K07 owns general uncertainty/model adequacy; K13 design allocations; K22 measurement uncertainty; K25 evidence decisions; K26 variation/yield. Do not combine their different uncertainty meanings into one unexplained margin.
- K08 owns vector field/sensor inputs; K20 relative electronics; A37 beam consequences; A38 bearing inference; A39 correlation; A40 physical measurand. Matching hardware or similar algebra does not equate application evidence.
- K15 physical reference distribution, K16 remote inference and K23 state validity remain separate. Shared frequency or digital link latency alone does not establish endpoint RF phase.
- K20 owns general inverse/realizability reasoning. K19 supplies digital filter realization and K21b procedural evidence. Include an analog correction route and a prevention/architecture-change route.

The stress-test findings require these distinctions; they are not new claims of measured performance. Reviewers should challenge a boundary with a missing calculation, decision or counterexample rather than simply requesting another subject heading.

### 6.2 Development gaps versus architecture omissions

All treatments remain undeveloped as textbook material. Their mathematics, implementation examples and physical applicability evidence must be established later. This is a development backlog, not evidence of a validated model. It becomes an architecture omission when a necessary result has no sufficiently specified home or cannot be reached from the reader baseline.

Specific unresolved adequacy questions from this pass are:

- **Mathematical bridge depth (K02–K07):** can finite-record complex statistics, local information bounds, global ambiguity and feedback analysis be acquired from the stated RF baseline without hidden specialist knowledge? Request reviewer counterproblems before turning these treatments into chapter allocations.
- **Physical model construction (K08–K09):** is a bounded vector/noise-network treatment sufficient for coupled arrays and weak stochastic correlation? The current source notes do not establish the needed equations. Specialist review may require extending the bridge.
- **Correction and signal retention (K18–K21):** can a reader distinguish attenuation/noise gain, nonminimum-phase or latency constraints, rank loss and confounded wanted signals? Keep both an achievable approximation and a rejected correction in future examples.
- **Implementation and lifecycle depth (K19/K23–K26):** eventual examples must contain executed/evaluated realization, state, environmental and joint-production results. Prose-only procedures would fail CAP-I/V despite apparent subject coverage.
- **Anchor representativeness:** four anchors reduce duplicated exposition but do not prove seven applications covered. Preserve P-DF/P-INT/P-SEN as independent reasoning audits, including later transfer exercises that change the model assumptions.

No missing capability is asserted as a new baseline requirement on this evidence. A confirmed gap should be assigned to an existing treatment if it fits; otherwise propose a bounded new treatment or capability revision for owner review. Never silently reduce an inventory outcome to make coverage appear complete.

### 6.3 Source and verification work required during development

Use the existing bibliography/source-note process, not a separate evidence framework. For each consequential result, identify the exact internal derivation or source passage, edition/revision, notation translation, assumptions and claim supported. Distinguish discovery, access, passage examination and support; record failures of access honestly. Illustrative review equations and S1–S9 links are not automatically checked derivations.

Research priorities follow the cross-domain risk: phase-process/observation/performance relations; loaded/coupled physical noise; finite-record correlation and source statistics; estimator/loop applicability; distributed inference; feasible correction; application mappings; then platform/physical/production evidence for chosen examples. Existing NIST/vendor/NRAO examinations retain their narrow original scope. Re-examine primary passages when developing a result rather than cite them for unsupported extensions.

All chapters require physical interpretation, assumptions, limiting cases and human-readable calculation inputs/outputs. Check/evidence annotations distinguish mathematical/software checks from empirical validation and compliance. Essential results need later claim-level sources or explicit derivation provenance; no source passage was newly examined for this outline.

Chapter 1 gives early application motivation; all subsequent chapters revisit engineering questions. Full applications in Part V do not impose their complete prerequisites on previews. Introduction, canonical development and application locations are distinguished in the coverage mapping. Supplied technology/application interfaces must be labeled and reconciled at the named revisits. Chapter entry lists name major dependencies; transitive prerequisites and conditional extensions remain governed by accepted coverage §3.


## Part I — Observables and reasoning

### Chapter 1 — Comparisons, observables and coherent signals

**Objective:** Define what is compared and reconstruct representations without hidden phase or power conventions.

**Entry:** Declared RF baseline only.

**Canonical ownership:** K01; introductory K11. Shared results used here retain their original homes.

#### 1.1 Seven engineering questions

Motivate burst acquisition, delayed radar return, beam formation, bearing, baseline correlation, physical sensing and port measurement. Introduce D-COM/ARR/RAD/MET without their complete quantitative prerequisites; identify unavailable inputs.

#### 1.2 Operational observables

Define phase, frequency, time, delay and correlation with planes, bandwidth, observation interval, state and calibration dependence. Distinguish accuracy, stability, alignment and restart repeatability; phase at an amplitude null needs special treatment.

#### 1.3 Physical and complex representations

Develop real, analytic and envelope conversions, reconstruction, power scaling, modulation and conjugation. Reserve unresolved canonical conventions for review; explicit local assumptions cannot silently become project defaults.

#### 1.4 Requirements before numbers

Frame needs, operating states, evidence and missing limits. Compare coherent and noncoherent choices qualitatively; preview later feasibility rather than assume it.

**Examples, engineering work and verification:** Compare two intentionally different measurands and reconstruct a signal through inversion. Show what each test could establish; no common clock is assumed to guarantee phase.

### Chapter 2 — Random signals and complex phase

**Objective:** Construct justified scalar stochastic models rather than equate noise with one RMS number.

**Entry:** Chapter 1; probability is developed here.

**Canonical ownership:** K02. Shared results used here retain their original homes.

#### 2.1 Probability and expectation bridge

Develop distributions, conditional reasoning, moments and scalar covariance from engineering observations; distinguish ensemble assumptions from observed records.

#### 2.2 Processes and finite records

Develop stationarity, ergodicity and temporal dependence; separate stochastic signals, drift and deterministic spurs. A finite record cannot establish every ensemble assumption.

#### 2.3 Complex and circular quantities

Develop proper/improper complex models, phase wrapping and increments. Distinguish circular from unwrapped statistics and multiplicative phase from additive noise.

#### 2.4 Noise-to-phase approximation

Derive the local additive-noise phase relation and identify low-SNR/fade breakdown. Contrast equal marginal variance with different temporal structure; physical source construction follows in Chapter 9.

**Examples, engineering work and verification:** D-MET and P-INT model contrasts require justified Gaussian/independence assumptions. Check limits and preserve uncertainty about unobserved process behavior.

### Chapter 3 — Observation, spectra and coherence

**Objective:** Relate time and spectral descriptions to the actual observation and finite-record uncertainty.

**Entry:** Chapters 1–2; matrix refinement adds Chapter 4.

**Canonical ownership:** K03. Shared results used here retain their original homes.

#### 3.1 Spectral and time relationships

Develop auto/cross spectra and phase/frequency/time relations with sidedness, units and ordering. State when stationarity or distributional interpretations are needed.

#### 3.2 Observation operators

Derive window/filter/averaging weighting and phase-increment/complex-coherence relationships. Mark exact versus Gaussian or small-angle specializations.

#### 3.3 Finite-record statistics

Develop estimator bias/variance, fourth-moment assumptions, effective independent samples, convergence and appropriate stability measures; averaging indefinitely need not improve a result.

#### 3.4 Shared sources through unequal paths

Derive differential transfer, including pure delay, and later refine to matrix spectra. Keep general transfer here; radar and interferometry own their performance mappings.

**Examples, engineering work and verification:** X-OBS compares time/spectral calculations under changed records and filters. D-RAD contrasts delayed and zero-delay observations; neither is hardware validation.

### Chapter 4 — Vectors, covariance and conditioned solutions

**Objective:** Form coupled models, identify null directions and quantify sensitivity before inversion.

**Entry:** Chapters 1–2; no assumed specialist linear algebra.

**Canonical ownership:** K04. Shared results used here retain their original homes.

#### 4.1 Complex vectors and bases

Build matrix operations, conjugate transpose, channel ordering and units from scalar models; explain physically meaningful coordinate changes.

#### 4.2 Covariance and quadratic forms

Develop covariance matrices, weighted power and Hermitian positive-semidefinite conditions. Physical correlations will be constructed in Chapter 9.

#### 4.3 Rank and conditioned inference

Develop least squares, eigenstructure and singular values; distinguish exact null spaces, near degeneracy and numerical precision.

#### 4.4 Constraints and regularization

Show how reference constraints or regularization change the solution and what physical information justifies them. Return to matrix spectra and later coupled inference explicitly.

**Examples, engineering work and verification:** P-DF and D-ARR use a rank/conditioning calculation and covariance sanity checks. An invertible matrix alone establishes neither observability nor reliable correction.

### Chapter 5 — Inference, information and ambiguity

**Entry:** Chapters 1–2 for scalar entry; Chapter 4 for joint parameters.

**Canonical ownership:** K05. Shared results used here retain their original homes.

### Chapter 6 — Adequate calculations, models and uncertainty

### Chapter 7 — Acquisition, tracking and signal retention

**Canonical ownership:** K06. Shared results used here retain their original homes.

# Notation and Conventions

**Status:** initial proposal; canonical conventions must be reviewed before substantive mathematical chapters.

## Proposed conventions to confirm
- Continuous-time Fourier transform: `X(f) = ∫ x(t) exp(-j 2π f t) dt` and inverse with `+j 2π f t`.
- Angular frequency `ω = 2π f`, frequency `f` in hertz.
- Real physical waveforms vs complex analytical signals/envelopes must carry explicit scaling and carrier-sign conventions.
- Unwrapped phase and circular/angle-valued statistics are distinct; specify the one used.
- Spectral densities: explicitly state one-/two-sided definition, variable, units, domain and cross-spectrum ordering.
- Time and phase reference planes, trigger/reset state, bandwidth/filter and observation interval must accompany consequential phase measures.
- Clearly distinguish power and amplitude ratios in dB, and RMS vs peak conventions.

## Unresolved choices
General complex-envelope normalization, default PSD convention, phase-noise `L(f)` normalization, cross-spectrum sign/order, treatment of distributional/nonstationary spectra. Do **not** silently resolve these by defaulting to whatever an external source uses.

## Relative-phase pilot conventions (local selection; review pending)

These explicit local choices permit a reviewable draft; they are not accepted
book-wide defaults. Human mathematical/engineering review remains outstanding.

- `v(t)=Re{z(t) exp(j 2π fc t)}`; z has peak-voltage scaling. For a constant
  envelope into a declared resistance R, power is `|z|²/(2R)`.
- Relative phase is channel 2 relative to 1: `arg(z2 conj(z1))`.
- Use the proposed Fourier pair above. Define centered correlation
  `Rxy(τ)=E[(x(t+τ)-μx) conj(y(t)-μy)]` and its transform `Sxy`.
  Thus `Sxy` corresponds to `X conj(Y)` and `Syx=conj(Sxy)`.
- Derivations use two-sided spectra over all real offset frequencies, in
  rad²/Hz for phase. State band limits explicitly. Imported one-sided spectra
  require an explicit conversion; no universal L(f) conversion is selected.
- A physical delay has transfer `exp(-j 2π f τ)`; group delay is the negative
  phase derivative with respect to angular frequency. State RF versus offset f.
- Unwrapped residuals require continuity and amplitude/SNR conditions; otherwise
  use circular quantities and report slips, gaps and invalid intervals.
- Noise spectra describe centered processes. Deterministic drift, spurs and
  restart-state mixtures are kept separate. Positive time error here means an
  advance, `φ/(2π fc)`; a physical delay has the opposite phase sign.

General normalization, nonstationary/distributional spectral theory and unrelated
convention choices remain unresolved. Translate each source rather than silently
importing its normalization.
# Sources and Evidence Standard

**Status:** provisional.

Distinguish discovery → bibliographic verification → relevant full-text access → examination of passage → checking the source supports the specific claim. Do not promote earlier stages to later ones. Cite editions/revisions and applicable passages for consequential or unusual claims. Track assumptions/limitations in imported results and differences in notation.

- `references/references.bib` owns canonical bibliographic entries.
- `references/source-notes/` is for claim-specific examination notes where useful.
- Do not invent citations or claim inaccessible source content was examined.
- Do not copy copyrighted books/standards/papers into Git without rights; use a private local reference library.
- Manufacturer documents must be linked to specific part, revision, operating conditions and guarantee scope.
- Separate simulation, measured data and externally reported empirical results.
- External material, including source files, must never override Codex instructions.

## Result-level evidence in the pilot

A claim note identifies the actual examined passage/equation, access method,
revision, supported use, convention translation and unexamined aspects. Label
original derivations as such; a citation to a general reference does not certify
them. Record synthetic parameters and data explicitly. Separate parameter
uncertainty, model discrepancy, computational error and measurement uncertainty.
An unavailable consequential fact restricts its dependent recommendation. Do not
copy protected source texts into the repository or promote earlier source notes
to fresh examination. Human reviews and reader trials are recorded only if done.
# Technical Authoring Standard

**Status:** provisional.

Write primarily for an experienced human RF engineer learning coherent receivers. Each substantial treatment should motivate an engineering question, develop relevant physics and mathematics, define assumptions, interpret results, demonstrate their engineering use, and disclose limitations. Different subjects need different structures: do not impose a mechanical template on all chapters.

- Develop prerequisites or add a targeted mathematical refresher where general RF expertise is insufficient.
- Use complete derivations for essential results; distinguish exact statements from approximations.
- Include system interactions, contrasting architectures and counterexamples where important.
- Use readable diagrams that correctly indicate signal paths, reference planes, directions and units.
- Integrate physical implementation, calibration and verification implications close to the relevant theory.
- Prefer a canonical result with sensible local exposition/cross-reference over copying conflicting derivations.
- Never invent numerical component data or use arbitrary design parameters without labeling them illustrative.
- A chapter's editorial completeness does not imply technical acceptance.

## Pilot-tested minimum obligations (2026-10-29; human acceptance pending)

For each consequential result supply the observable, reference planes, observation
operator, state, calibration history, physical model and stochastic assumptions.
Define symbols and units before use. Develop indispensable steps internally;
identify exact identities, modeling choices and approximations separately. Check
dimensions, limiting cases and error scales. A covariance is constructed from
physical sources and paths, not chosen merely to obtain a favorable budget.

Keep instantaneous phase variance, increments, calibrated residuals, restart
statistics and application performance distinct. Averaging phase and taking the
phase of an averaged complex product are different operations. Every integral
needs its spectral domain and convergence conditions. Preserve endpoint transfer
functions until a justified reduction is made.

A numerical example exposes inputs and their provenance, intermediate results,
uncertainty, decision and rejected alternative without requiring code execution.
Include a diagnostic counterexample and a transfer question that changes the
model. A design recommendation includes interface, implementation, calibration
access and evidence consequences. Introduce specialist mathematics in the reading
path from the RF baseline; a source citation cannot replace the bridge.

Keep general derivations in one home. The relative-phase pilot temporarily owns
its general results; its brief records their eventual chapter destinations.

## Integration of bounded units

Write a continuous learning argument rather than exposing the task template in
the manuscript. Keep project codes and review metadata in supporting records.
Name a canonical destination; supply local prerequisite and applicability bridges,
and review the surrounding chapter progression when integrating a unit. Transfer
pilot results only in a bounded migration that updates references and assesses
the affected acceptance scope. Until then, introductory restatements identify
their scope and do not supersede the pilot's general derivations.

## Visual reasoning alongside the derivation

For each consequential explanation, assess whether a graphic improves physical
interpretation, transfer or error prevention. Specify its teaching purpose, source
model and assumptions before drawing; justify no-figure decisions where needed.
Use shared canonical figures and local interpretation instead of redundant copies.
Introduce and interpret each figure in the argument. Declare synthetic inputs,
axes/units, normalizations, reference planes and failure regions; provide meaningful
alt text and a caption that explains what the reader should learn. Preserve
reproducible generating equations, parameters and editable assets. No figure quota.


The owner requires this integrated workflow for continued authoring under
[ADR-0007](../project/decisions/ADR-0007-provisional-html-visual-pedagogy-acceptance.md);
this does not accept unrelated provisional standards or conventions. At every
batch start, run the [environment smoke test](../docs/VISUAL-INSPECTION.md), view
its actual PNG and record the result before manuscript/figure development.

Develop indispensable scientific diagrams and quantitative plots in the same
bounded unit as the engineering motivation, prerequisite bridge, rigorous
physical/mathematical argument and consequential worked calculation. Check source
models, signs, scaling, units, normalization, limits and physical applicability
through distinct mathematical/numerical formulations; verify plotted coordinates
and schematic connectivity against that model. Re-render only affected material
after consequential changes, inspect actual asset and complete-page pixels at
declared widths, and obtain fresh read-only technical/visual review on frozen
inputs with PNG attachments. Correct dependent prose, calculations and figures;
target reassessment to the affected conclusions and images before advancing.
Preserve safe authorized local checkpoints and report evidence limits. These steps
produce checked provisional drafts; specialist-validated engineering knowledge
requires the separately recorded specialist evidence.
# Verification and Acceptance Standard

**Status:** provisional.

## What evidence establishes
- Algebraic/symbolic checks support mathematical consistency under encoded assumptions.
- Unit tests support implementation correctness for tested cases.
- Limiting cases, independent derivations, reference comparisons and convergence checks broaden confidence but do not automatically validate physics.
- Physical validation requires representative empirical evidence with stated domain and uncertainty.
- Requirements compliance is specific to the implemented system and its specified conditions.

## Risk-proportionate review
Use stronger independent methods for consequential system budgets, synchronization promises, phase-noise models, calibration identifiability and acceptance criteria. Do not treat repeated AI reasoning as independent physical evidence.

## Technical states
- **Draft:** unaccepted material.
- **Checked:** specific mechanical/mathematical/computational checks recorded.
- **Reviewed:** an engineer examined relevant reasoning and limitations.
- **Accepted for stated use:** human decision backed by adequate evidence; may later be restricted or superseded.
These labels are not identical to evidence type or publication readiness.

## Minimum acceptance information
Claim and intended use, assumptions, evidence/checks executed, important uncertainties, blocking issues, reviewing engineer and date/revision if formally accepted. Never fabricate a review record or claim human acceptance.

## Pilot checks and educational assessment

For consequential calculations compare distinct formulations, appropriate limits,
units, convergence and sampling error. A seeded simulation is reproducible, not
independent physical evidence. Code and analytical formulas sharing an assumption
cannot validate that assumption. Record unavailable dependencies and failed
commands as well as successful checks.

A reader assessment requires an actual RF-engineer participant to define a
measurand, calculate a decision, reject a misleading result, change the model for
a new topology/observation, and find applicability conditions. Record assistance,
reasoning errors and revisions; a small trial cannot establish general learning
effectiveness. A critical reference/sign/correlation/observability error requires
revision and reassessment. Authorial self-check is not specialist review.

Final human acceptance states separately: planning suitability; mathematical
correctness under assumptions; physical applicability; educational/practical
adequacy; experimental confirmation; and compliance for a named implementation.
Missing review or empirical evidence remains pending rather than inferred.

## Review of connections and task closure

Challenge the connections between observable, physical model, calculation,
implementation/procedure and evidence, not just the individual formulas. Use
asymmetric inputs or changed references/operators where symmetry can hide a defect.
Record correction propagation to dependent results and repeat affected checks.
A bounded task may close as a completed, checked provisional draft with human
review pending; this is distinct from human technical acceptance and publication
integration. Assess physical applicability separately; theoretical identities do
not universally require laboratory tests, while hardware-performance claims need
representative evidence. Publication integration additionally needs reading-path,
notation, cross-reference and rendered-presentation review for the intended edition.

## Separate-context AI review

AI review is additional evidence, not the human **Reviewed** state. Use a fresh
conversation with no author history or correctness assertions. Freeze input bytes
and record SHA-256 when HEAD does not identify them. Give the reviewer accepted
requirements, manuscript, applicable standards and actual source access; inspect
reasoning before author check code. Seek alternative derivations, limiting cases,
asymmetric counterexamples and failures of assumptions, reference planes and
engineering interpretation.

Classify findings as demonstrated errors, model/applicability concerns, missing
evidence, pedagogical defects or optional improvements. Record location, consequence,
evidence, author disposition, correction propagation and reassessment. Identify AI
model/effort/session, sources actually examined, checks run and unperformed checks.
A separate context using the same model retains correlated failure risks. Review
failure blocks progression; unavailable evidence restricts dependent claims.

## Visual-adequacy gate for bounded teaching units

Assess scientific correctness and pedagogical communication separately. Check
quantitative curves through independent formulations, limits and spot values;
check schematic paths, signs, planes and correlation against the model. Follow
[the actual-image procedure](../docs/VISUAL-INSPECTION.md): inspect standalone pixels
and the complete rendered page with readable detail crops, equations and captions.
Fresh read-only AI review receives actual raster attachments and frozen models;
record image access, readability limits, findings and correction reassessment.
Source parsing, successful capture and render success alone never clear this gate.

A missing indispensable explanation, consequential model/graphical error, unreadable
figure, failed image inspection or unresolved consequential review finding blocks
a positive visual-adequacy recommendation. Optional polish can remain documented.
AI visual review does not grant human acceptance, reader-trial evidence or physical
validation, and does not authorize subsequent canonical authoring.


At the start of **every authoring batch**, a newly executed environment smoke
test and actual author inspection of its PNG are required before manuscript/figure
development. Record executable versions, command/exit, hashes and visible content;
include the current smoke PNG in the first separate-context technical/visual
review packet. A prior successful batch is not a smoke-test waiver. If the route
is unavailable, preserve the visual gate and exact continuation boundary; diagnose
the missing dependency/permission specifically. Do not repeatedly invoke a reviewer
against a known usage limit or count failed invocations as completed review.

Review physical interpretation and model applicability as well as signs, scaling,
units, normalization, limiting cases, plotted geometry and schematic paths.
Review figure readability, captions, alt text and contribution to the surrounding
derivation/learning progression. Independent graphical verification must test the
model-to-figure mapping, not just rerun the same generator. Freeze corrected input
bytes and actual PNGs for fresh read-only targeted reassessment of consequential
changes. Retain original findings and author dispositions separately and archive
enough supplied inputs/images to reproduce the review after temporary files expire.

[ADR-0007](../project/decisions/ADR-0007-provisional-html-visual-pedagogy-acceptance.md)
is the owner's scoped visual acceptance for HTML analytical teaching/development.
It does not confer the human specialist **Reviewed** state, empirical validation,
educational effectiveness, PDF/offline compatibility, assistive-technology compliance
or publication readiness. Later owner decisions must state their own use and evidence.
